title: Source Selection and Evaluation
summary: Source selection is the process of evaluating proposals against the factors stated in the solicitation and selecting the offeror whose proposal represents the best value to the Government. The two approaches are lowest price technically acceptable and trade-off, and the choice between them is a judgment about whether technical superiority is worth paying for. Boards test this hard because it is where integrity, documentation and protest risk all meet.

sections.heading: LPTA versus trade-off
sections.body:
Best value is the outcome that in the Government's estimation provides the greatest overall benefit in response to the requirement. Two approaches deliver it.

- Lowest price technically acceptable. Award goes to the lowest-priced proposal that meets or exceeds the stated acceptability standards. Technical factors are evaluated acceptable or unacceptable, there is no trade-off between price and technical merit, and proposals are not ranked for technical superiority. Use it when the requirement is well defined, performance risk is minimal, and there is no value in paying more for higher performance.
- Trade-off. Permits trade-offs among cost or price and non-cost factors, and allows award to other than the lowest-priced or other than the highest technically rated proposal. Use it when the requirement is less definite, development risk exists, performance risk varies, or superior technical performance is worth the added cost.

The solicitation must state the relative importance of all factors and subfactors, and whether non-cost factors combined are significantly more important than, approximately equal to, or significantly less important than cost or price.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.103-1 (trade-off, was 15.101-1); RFO FAR 15.103-2 (LPTA, was 15.101-2).

sections.heading: Evaluation factors
sections.body:
Factors are the Government's statement of what will decide the award, and everything that follows is bound by them.

The rules:
- Price or cost to the Government must be evaluated in every source selection.
- The quality of the product or service must be evaluated through one or more non-cost factors - past performance, compliance with requirements, technical excellence, management capability, personnel qualifications, prior experience.
- Past performance must be evaluated in competitive acquisitions expected to exceed the threshold set by regulation, unless the KO documents why it is not an appropriate factor.
- Small business participation and subcontracting factors are evaluated when required.
- Factors and significant subfactors must represent the key areas of importance and emphasis to be considered, and must support meaningful comparison and discrimination between competing proposals.

And the hard rule: the Government evaluates proposals based solely on the factors and subfactors specified in the solicitation. Unstated criteria are a protest waiting to happen. Experience is what an offeror has done; past performance is how well they did it - boards ask that distinction directly.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.104 (was 15.304); RFO FAR 15.202 (was 15.305).

sections.heading: Clarifications, communications and discussions
sections.body:
Three kinds of exchanges after receipt of proposals, and candidates lose points by blurring them.

- Clarifications are limited exchanges when award without discussions is contemplated. They address minor or clerical errors, or let an offeror clarify adverse past performance information it has not previously had an opportunity to address. They need not be offered to all offerors, and no proposal revision is allowed.
- Communications are exchanges before the competitive range is established. They are limited to offerors whose past performance is the determining factor preventing inclusion, and to offerors whose inclusion or exclusion is uncertain. They may address ambiguities and enhance Government understanding, but may not cure deficiencies or material omissions or materially alter the proposal.
- Discussions are negotiations after the competitive range is established, with the intent of allowing revision. They must be meaningful: the KO must indicate to each offeror in the range its deficiencies, significant weaknesses, and adverse past performance it has not had an opportunity to address. They are held with all offerors in the range, and final proposal revisions are requested with a common cutoff date.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.204 (was 15.306).

sections.heading: The competitive range and the decision
sections.body:
If the KO decides to conduct discussions, the KO establishes a competitive range comprising all of the most highly rated proposals, based on their ratings against all evaluation criteria, unless it is further reduced for efficiency. An excluded offeror gets prompt written notice and may request a preaward debriefing.

The source selection decision is the SSA's. It must be independent, based on a comparative assessment of proposals against all criteria in the solicitation, and documented - including the rationale for any business judgments and trade-offs, and the benefits associated with additional costs.

Roles:
- SSEB - evaluates proposals against the factors and documents strengths, weaknesses, deficiencies and risk.
- SSAC - reviews SSEB results and provides comparative analysis and an award recommendation on larger acquisitions.
- SSA - makes the decision; on many acquisitions the KO is the SSA.
- KO - runs the process, is the sole point of contact with offerors, and signs the contract.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.204; RFO FAR 15.201 (was 15.303); RFO FAR 15.205 (was 15.308).

sections.heading: Debriefings and integrity
sections.body:
Debriefings close the loop and, done well, reduce protests.

- Preaward debriefing: available to an offeror excluded from the competitive range, on written request within 3 days after receipt of the notice of exclusion. It covers the evaluation of significant elements of that offeror's proposal, a summary of the rationale for exclusion, and reasonable responses to relevant questions. It does not disclose the number or identity of other offerors or anything about their proposals.
- Postaward debriefing: available on written request received within 3 days after the offeror received notice of award. It includes the evaluation of significant weaknesses or deficiencies, the overall evaluated cost or price and technical rating of both the awardee and the debriefed offeror, the overall ranking if one was developed, a summary of the rationale for award, and reasonable responses to relevant questions.
- Never disclosed: point-by-point comparisons with other proposals, and anything exempt from release - trade secrets, privileged manufacturing processes, confidential commercial and financial information, and the names of individuals providing past performance information.

Procurement integrity runs underneath all of it.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.206-2 (was 15.505); RFO FAR 15.301 (was 15.506); RFO FAR 3.104.

sections.heading: Traps and how boards probe it
sections.body:
Traps:
- Evaluating on unstated criteria, or applying a stated factor differently than the solicitation described.
- Conducting "discussions" and calling them clarifications. If an offeror is given the opportunity to revise its proposal, they were discussions, and they must be held with everyone in the competitive range.
- Failing to make discussions meaningful by omitting a significant weakness.
- An SSA decision document that recites ratings without explaining the trade-off - "Offeror A is higher rated and higher priced, therefore award to A" is not a rationale.
- Leadership pressure to reach a preferred outcome. Boards will put this in a scenario on purpose.

How they probe it: expect a competitive range scenario with five proposals, a trade-off question with a higher-priced superior offeror, a definition question on the three exchanges, and an ethics scenario where a senior official pushes you. On that last one the answer is that you document the direction, state the legal and regulatory basis for your position, involve counsel and the competition advocate, and if directed to act unlawfully you do not sign - the warrant is personal and so is the accountability.

Cite: RFO FAR 15.204; RFO FAR 15.205; RFO FAR 3.104.

board_angles.q: When would you use LPTA versus trade-off?
board_angles.a: LPTA when the requirement is well defined, performance risk is minimal and there is no value in paying more for better performance; trade-off when the requirement is less definite, risk varies among offerors, or technical superiority is worth the added cost.

board_angles.q: Explain the three types of exchanges after receipt of proposals.
board_angles.a: Clarifications are limited exchanges when award without discussions is contemplated and allow no proposal revision; communications occur before the competitive range is set and cannot cure deficiencies; discussions occur after the competitive range is established, must be meaningful, and allow proposal revisions.

board_angles.q: How do you establish the competitive range?
board_angles.a: If I decide to conduct discussions I include all of the most highly rated proposals based on their ratings against all the stated evaluation criteria, and I may reduce it further for efficiency, notifying excluded offerors promptly in writing.

board_angles.q: What is the difference between experience and past performance?
board_angles.a: Experience is what the offeror has done - the type, size and complexity of work performed; past performance is how well they performed it, including quality, schedule, cost control and customer satisfaction.

board_angles.q: What must the SSA's decision document contain?
board_angles.a: An independent, comparative assessment of proposals against all the solicitation's source selection criteria, with the rationale for every business judgment and trade-off made - including the benefits associated with any additional cost.

board_angles.q: What can you not tell an unsuccessful offeror in a debriefing?
board_angles.a: No point-by-point comparison with other proposals, and nothing exempt from release - trade secrets, privileged manufacturing processes, confidential commercial and financial information, or the names of individuals who provided past performance information.
